spark.summary: BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs level by level, DFS explores depth-first for cycle detection and topological ordering, and Dijkstra uses a min-heap to find shortest paths in non-negative weighted graphs.
spark.keyTakeaway: Choosing the right traversal—O(V+E) BFS/DFS for structure and unweighted hops vs. O((V+E) log V) Dijkstra for weighted costs—powers everything from Bazel build DAGs and social graphs to network routing.

concept.whyItMatters: Real-world engineering problems—dependency resolution in package managers, microservice call-graph cycle detection, social network degrees of separation, and road/network latency routing—are all graph problems. Picking the wrong algorithm (like DFS for shortest paths or Dijkstra on negative weights) produces subtle bugs or exponential blowups.
whenToUse: BFS: finding shortest unweighted path (fewest hops), level-order traversal, or bidirectional search in social/network graphs
DFS: topological sorting of build/task DAGs (Kahn's or post-order), cycle detection (3-color marking), and finding strongly connected components (Tarjan's)
Dijkstra: computing single-source shortest paths in graphs with non-negative edge weights (network latency, road distances, weighted routing)
whenNotToUse: Dijkstra on graphs with negative edge weights—greedy relaxation locks in suboptimal distances; use Bellman-Ford (O(VE)) or SPFA instead
Unidirectional BFS on deep high-branching-factor graphs (e.g., b=10, depth=8 -> 10^8 nodes) when both source and target are known; use bidirectional BFS (2 * 10^4 nodes)
Plain Dijkstra on massive 2D/geo grids when a valid admissible heuristic exists; use A* to prune search space toward the goal
keyPoints: Complexity bounds: BFS and DFS run in O(V + E) time and O(V) space using an adjacency list; Dijkstra with a binary min-heap runs in O((V + E) log V) time.
Adjacency list vs. matrix: real sparse graphs (V=100,000, avg degree 10) take ~8 MB as an adjacency list vs. ~10 GB as an O(V^2) matrix.
3-color DFS cycle detection: marking nodes White (unvisited), Gray (in active recursion stack), and Black (finished) detects back-edges (cycles) in directed graphs in O(V + E).
Bidirectional BFS optimization: expanding simultaneously from source and target cuts search space from O(b^d) to O(2 * b^(d/2))—orders of magnitude faster for social/knowledge graphs.
Dijkstra greedy invariant: once a node is popped from the min-heap, its shortest distance is final—which holds strictly because all remaining edge weights are >= 0.

examples.title: Build-System Topological Sort & Cycle Detection (Bazel / Cargo)
examples.scenario: A monorepo with 18,000 packages suffered from silent circular dependency regressions and slow full rebuilds.
examples.outcome: Running 3-color DFS on the package dependency graph caught circular imports in <40 ms during pre-commit, while Kahn's topological sort scheduled independent build targets in parallel waves.

examples.title: Bidirectional BFS for Real-Time Professional Network Degrees
examples.scenario: Computing 4-hop connection paths on a 50M-user graph with average degree 120 using standard BFS visited >200M edges and timed out at 4.5 seconds.
examples.outcome: Switching to bidirectional BFS (expanding from the smaller frontier at each step) reduced visited nodes from ~1.7M to ~2,400 and dropped p99 query latency to 14 ms.

tradeOffs.pro: BFS guarantees the minimum-hop shortest path on the first visit to the target.
tradeOffs.con: BFS stores the entire frontier queue in memory (O(b^d) space), whereas DFS only stores the current path (O(d) space).

tradeOffs.pro: Dijkstra requires no domain heuristic and computes shortest paths to all reachable nodes from a single source.
tradeOffs.con: Explores uniformly in all directions; A* with an admissible heuristic (e.g., Euclidean/Haversine distance) visits 5x–50x fewer nodes for point-to-point routing.

tradeOffs.factor: Recursive DFS vs. Explicit Stack DFS
tradeOffs.pro: Recursive DFS is concise and natural for tree/DAG post-order and Tarjan's SCC.
tradeOffs.con: Deep graphs (V > 10,000 chain) overflow the OS call stack in Python/Java/C++, requiring an explicit iterative stack.

failureModes.name: Stack Overflow on Deep Chains in Recursive DFS
failureModes.description: A linear dependency chain of 50,000 nodes exceeds Python's 1,000-frame recursion limit or Java's ~1 MB thread stack, crashing the process.
failureModes.mitigation: Implement DFS iteratively using an explicit heap-allocated stack (collections.deque or ArrayDeque).

failureModes.name: Dijkstra Silent Wrong Answer on Negative Edges
failureModes.description: Applying Dijkstra to a currency-arbitrage or cost-rebate graph with negative edges finalizes a node too early and misses the true shortest path.
failureModes.mitigation: Validate all edge weights >= 0; if negative edges exist, run Bellman-Ford (which also detects negative cycles) or Johnson's algorithm.

failureModes.name: Infinite Loop from Missing Visited Set
failureModes.description: Forgetting to mark nodes visited *before* pushing onto a BFS queue (marking on pop instead) enqueues the same node up to O(E) times in dense graphs.
failureModes.mitigation: In BFS, always insert into the visited set at enqueue time; in Dijkstra, skip stale heap entries where popped_dist > dist[u].

failureModes.name: Memory Explosion from Adjacency Matrix
failureModes.description: Allocating a boolean[V][V] matrix for V=100,000 nodes consumes 10 GB of RAM before traversal even begins.
failureModes.mitigation: Represent sparse graphs with adjacency lists (CSR arrays or hash-map/slice lists) taking O(V + E) memory.

commonMistakes: Marking BFS nodes visited when popping from the queue instead of when pushing, causing duplicate queue entries and exponential slowdown.
Using DFS to find the shortest path in an unweighted graph—DFS finds *a* path, not the shortest path.
Attempting to decrease-key inside a standard library heap (Python heapq / Java PriorityQueue) which lacks O(log V) decrease-key; push a new (dist, node) tuple and ignore stale pops instead.
Using a binary visited boolean for directed cycle detection instead of 3-color (unvisited / visiting / visited) state—diamond DAGs are not cycles.
Forgetting to check for disconnected components by looping over all vertices 0..V-1 for topological sort or SCC.

sections.content:
## The idea

Graph traversal algorithms differ primarily in **frontier discipline**—the data structure controlling which discovered vertex is expanded next:

- **BFS (FIFO Queue)** expands vertices in strict increasing order of hop distance from the source, guaranteeing the shortest unweighted path in $O(V + E)$ time.
- **DFS (LIFO Stack)** plunges as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking, exposing ancestor/descendant relationships—ideal for cycle detection, topological sorting, and strongly connected components in $O(V + E)$ time.
- **Dijkstra (Min-Heap Priority Queue)** generalizes BFS to non-negative weighted graphs, always expanding the unfinalized vertex with the smallest cumulative cost $d[u]$ in $O((V + E) \log V)$ time.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace Dijkstra's lazy-deletion min-heap pattern on a 4-node network graph (`A -> B: 4`, `A -> C: 1`, `C -> B: 2`, `B -> D: 1`, `C -> D: 5`):

1. **Initialize**: Set `dist = {A: 0, B: inf, C: inf, D: inf}` and push `(0, A)` onto the min-heap.
2. **Pop `(0, A)`**: Relax neighbors: `dist[B] = 4`, push `(4, B)`; `dist[C] = 1`, push `(1, C)`.
3. **Pop `(1, C)`**: Since `1 == dist[C]`, expand `C`. Relax `C -> B` (`1 + 2 = 3 < 4`): update `dist[B] = 3` and push `(3, B)` (lazy duplicate—old `(4, B)` stays in heap). Relax `C -> D` (`1 + 5 = 6`): `dist[D] = 6`, push `(6, D)`.
4. **Pop `(3, B)`**: `3 == dist[B]`, expand `B`. Relax `B -> D` (`3 + 1 = 4 < 6`): update `dist[D] = 4`, push `(4, D)`.
5. **Pop `(4, B)` (stale) & `(4, D)`**: When `(4, B)` pops, `4 > dist[B] (3)`, so skip it in $O(1)$. Pop `(4, D)`, finalize `D` at shortest distance **4** (`A -> C -> B -> D`).

sections.content:
## High-leverage variants in systems

- **0-1 BFS (Deque)**: When edge weights are strictly `0` or `1` (e.g., same-rack vs. cross-rack network hops), push `0`-weight edges to the front of a `deque` and `1`-weight edges to the back. This achieves Dijkstra's result in linear $O(V + E)$ time without a heap.
- **Bidirectional BFS**: For point-to-point unweighted shortest paths with branching factor $b$ and distance $d$, searching from both `src` and `dst` reduces explored nodes from $b^d$ to $2 \cdot b^{d/2}$ (at $b=10, d=6$, that is $2{,}000$ nodes vs. $1{,}000{,}000$).
- **DAG Shortest Path**: If the graph is acyclic (verified by DFS), relax edges in topological order—handling even negative weights in $O(V + E)$ without Dijkstra or Bellman-Ford.

## Graph traversal and pathfinding comparison

| Algorithm | Frontier Structure | Time Complexity | Space | Negative Weights | Primary Use Case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **BFS** | FIFO Queue | O(V + E) | O(V) | N/A (unweighted) | Shortest hop count, level-order traversal |
| **DFS** | LIFO Stack | O(V + E) | O(V) | N/A | Topological sort, cycle detection, SCCs |
| **Dijkstra (Binary Heap)** | Min-Heap | O((V + E) log V) | O(V + E) | Fails | Single-source shortest path (w >= 0) |
| **A\* Search** | Min-Heap (g + h) | O((V + E) log V) worst | O(V) | Fails | Point-to-point routing with admissible heuristic |
| **Bellman-Ford** | Edge-list passes | O(V * E) | O(V) | Supported | Graphs with negative edges / cycle detection |

## Failure modes

- **Stale Heap Entries Not Skipped**: Without `if popped_dist > dist[u]: continue`, Dijkstra re-expands already finalized nodes and degrades to exponential time on dense graphs.
- **Integer Overflow on `INF + weight`**: Initializing `dist[v] = INT_MAX` and computing `INT_MAX + w` wraps around to a huge negative number in C++/Java; use `Long.MAX_VALUE / 2` or explicit infinity checks.
- **Recursive Stack Overflow**: Running recursive DFS on skewed graphs (e.g., 100,000-node linked chains) crashes Python (`RecursionError`) and JVM (`StackOverflowError`).
- **Incorrect Cycle Detection in Directed Graphs**: Using a single `visited` set instead of 3-color (`UNVISITED`, `VISITING`, `VISITED`) flags diamond DAGs (`A -> B -> D`, `A -> C -> D`) as false cycles.

## Production implementation patterns

In Java and Python, standard priority queues (`PriorityQueue` and `heapq`) do not support $O(\log V)$ `decrease_key`.

- **Lazy Deletion Pattern**: Push `(new_dist, v)` onto the heap whenever a shorter path is found, and discard popped pairs where `d > dist[v]`. Memory stays bounded at $O(E)$ heap entries, and real-world cache locality beats theoretical Fibonacci heaps ($O(E + V \log V)$) due to zero pointer chasing.
- **Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) Arrays**: For static graphs with millions of edges (e.g., road networks), store neighbors in two flat integer arrays (`offsets[V+1]` and `edges[E]`) instead of `HashMap<Integer, List<Edge>>`, cutting RAM usage by 5x–10x and eliminating GC pressure.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Use adjacency lists (or CSR arrays for static large graphs) instead of $O(V^2)$ matrices for sparse graphs.
- [ ] In BFS, mark nodes `visited` **at enqueue time**, never at dequeue time.
- [ ] Use iterative stacks for DFS on graphs that may exceed ~1,000 nodes in depth.
- [ ] Use 3-color (`White`/`Gray`/`Black`) tracking for directed cycle detection and Kahn's algorithm or post-order DFS for topological sort.
- [ ] In Dijkstra, verify all edge weights are $\ge 0$, use lazy deletion (`if d > dist[u]: continue`), and guard against `INF` overflow.
- [ ] Consider bidirectional BFS or A* whenever both source and target are known on large graphs.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs level by level, DFS explores depth-first for cycle detection and topological ordering, and Dijkstra uses a min-heap to find shortest paths in non-negative weighted graphs.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: DFS (LIFO Stack) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Dijkstra (Min-Heap).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Dijkstra (Min-Heap) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Implement DFS iteratively using an explicit heap-allocated stack (collections.deque or ArrayDeque).

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Choosing the right traversal—O(V+E) BFS/DFS for structure and unweighted hops vs. O((V+E) log V) Dijkstra for weighted costs—powers everything from Bazel build DAGs and social graphs to network routing.
Avoid trap: Marking BFS nodes visited when popping from the queue instead of when pushing, causing duplicate queue entries and exponential slowdown.
Avoid trap: Using DFS to find the shortest path in an unweighted graph—DFS finds *a* path, not the shortest path.
When to reach for it: BFS: finding shortest unweighted path (fewest hops), level-order traversal, or bidirectional search in social/network graphs
When to reach for it: DFS: topological sorting of build/task DAGs (Kahn's or post-order), cycle detection (3-color marking), and finding strongly connected components (Tarjan's)
